Description: International think‑tank that published the *Limits to Growth* report in 1972.
Supporting_Text: 1972 was also the year that the seminal Limits to Growth report of the Club of Rome was published.

Name: United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP)
Role: Institutionalised environmental concerns within the UN system, prompting many governments to create dedicated environment ministries and consider non‑GDP metrics.
Description: UN agency created to coordinate global environmental activities.
Supporting_Text: It created the United Nations Environmental Programme, which stimulated governments all over the world to set up environmental ministries.

Name: United Nations World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED)
Role: Popularised the concept of sustainable development, providing a narrative that links environmental health, social equity, and economic policy.
Description: UN commission that produced the 1987 *Our Common Future* (Brundtland) report.
Supporting_Text: the seminal publication by the United NationsWorld Commission on Environment and Development (WCED) in 1987.

Name: Eurostat
Role: Started work on Sustainable Development Indicators in 2005, contributing statistical foundations for measuring progress beyond GDP.
Description: Statistical office of the European Union responsible for producing European-wide statistics. Statistical office of the European Union, headquartered in Luxembourg. Statistical office of the European U...
Supporting_Text: Eurostat (the statistical office of the European Union) started work on Sustainable Development Indicators in 2005.

Name: Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress (CMEPSP)
Role: Produced the Stiglitz Report, a landmark document advocating the replacement of GDP with broader well‑being indicators.
Description: French presidential commission created in 2009 to review GDP and propose new metrics.
Supporting_Text: In 2009, Nicolas Sarkozy, President of France, set up the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress.

Name: Working Group for Statistics of Sustainable Development (WGSSD)
Role: Advanced methodological convergence for measuring progress beyond GDP across UN agencies and statistical offices.
Description: UN‑led expert group (2004‑2009) that worked on harmonising sustainable‑development statistics.
Supporting_Text: the Working Group for Statistics of Sustainable Development (WGSSD) (2004-2009)

Name: Task Force for Sustainable Development (TFSD)
Role: Continued the work of WGSSD, promoting coherent global metrics that incorporate environmental and social values.
Description: UN‑led task force (2009‑2014) focused on sustainable‑development indicators.
Supporting_Text: the Task Force for Sustainable Development (TFSD) (2009-2014)

Name: United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UN‑ECE)
Role: Co‑led the harmonisation efforts (WGSSD, TFSD) that underpinned the development of Beyond‑GDP indicators.
Description: Regional UN body based in Geneva, Switzerland.
Supporting_Text: which were led by the UN‑ECE, OECD and Eurostat.

Name: Gallup World Poll
Role: Conducts large‑scale surveys on subjective well‑being across many countries, supplying data that feeds alternative well‑being metrics beyond GDP.
Description: A global public‑opinion polling initiative run by Gallup, a U.S. analytics and advisory firm.
Supporting_Text: The Gallup World Poll started in 2005 with 26 countries and had expanded to around 140 countries by 2018.

Name: Daniel Kahneman
Role: Advocates the hedonic‑psychology approach to well‑being and co‑developed the "U‑index" for quantifying negative experiences, influencing how affective dimensions are measured in Beyond‑GDP frameworks.
Description: Psychologist, Nobel laureate in Economics (2002), and a founding figure of behavioural economics.
Supporting_Text: The proponents of which include Daniel Kahneman, a psychologist, one of the founders of behavioural economics and winner of the Nobel Prize in economics in 2002.

Name: Alan Krueger
Role: Co‑author with Kahneman of the 2006 paper that proposes the "U‑index" for measuring time spent on unpleasant activities, contributing methodological tools for well‑being measurement.
Description: Economist and public‑policy scholar known for work on happiness economics.
Supporting_Text: Kahneman and Krueger (2006) suggest that any episode can be quantified as positive or negative.

Name: European Value Survey
Role: Provides longitudinal data on subjective well‑being and related attitudes, supporting the development of indicator‑based Beyond‑GDP measurement systems.
Description: A large‑scale, cross‑national survey programme that collects data on values, attitudes, and well‑being in European societies.
Supporting_Text: From 1981, academic groups started to work on the European Value Survey and World Value Survey in order to compare various SWB and other attitudes over multiple countries.

Name: World Value Survey
Role: Supplies comparative data on life evaluations and other well‑being dimensions that feed into alternative metrics beyond GDP.
Description: An international research project that surveys public values and beliefs across many countries worldwide.
Supporting_Text: From 1981, academic groups started to work on the European Value Survey and World Value Survey in order to compare various SWB and other attitudes over multiple countries.

Name: Nordhaus
Role: Co‑author of the early green‑accounting index (MEW) that added leisure and subtracted environmental damage, pioneering the incorporation of nature’s value into welfare measurement.
Description: Yale economist who co‑created the Measure of Economic Welfare (MEW).
Supporting_Text: the Measure of Economic Welfare was created by Yale economists Nordhaus and Tobin.

Name: Tobin
Role: Co‑author of the early green‑accounting index (MEW) that added leisure and subtracted environmental damage, pioneering the incorporation of nature’s value into welfare measurement.
Description: Yale economist who co‑created the Measure of Economic Welfare (MEW).
Supporting_Text: the Measure of Economic Welfare was created by Yale economists Nordhaus and Tobin.

Name: Daly
Role: Co‑developer of ISEW, a green‑accounting aggregate that later evolved into the Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI), integrating ecological limits into economic measurement.
Description: Economist (Herman Daly) who co‑proposed the Index for Sustainable Economic Welfare (ISEW).
Supporting_Text: The MEW methodology inspired the Index for Sustainable Economic Welfare (ISEW), which was proposed in 1989 by Daly and Cobb.

Name: Cobb
Role: Co‑developer of ISEW, a green‑accounting aggregate that later evolved into the Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI), integrating ecological limits into economic measurement.
Description: Economist (John Cobb) who co‑proposed the Index for Sustainable Economic Welfare (ISEW).
Supporting_Text: The MEW methodology inspired the Index for Sustainable Economic Welfare (ISEW), which was proposed in 1989 by Daly and Cobb.

Name: Roefie Hueting
Role: Proposed a green‑accounting method that uses environmental limits as the foundation, directly quantifying the maximum national income compatible with sustainability.
Description: Economist who introduced the Sustainable National Income (SNI) approach.
Supporting_Text: A different, rather unique, approach was proposed in 1974 by Roefie Hueting: Sustainable National Income.

Name: John Hicks
Role: Provided the theoretical basis for the capital approach to green accounting, linking maintenance of capital stocks to sustainable income measurement.
Description: Economist who defined real (Hicksian) income and contributed to capital‑based green accounting.
Supporting_Text: John Hicks, back in 1939, defined real income as the maximum amount that could be spent on consumption without reducing the capacity to maintain the same consumption stream over time.

Name: United Nations University
Role: Led the creation of the Inclusive Wealth Index, a comprehensive measure that aggregates natural, human, and produced capital to reflect the true wealth of nations beyond GDP.
Description: UN research and training institute that developed the Inclusive Wealth Index (IWI).
Supporting_Text: The United Nations University, under the leadership of Partha Dasgupta, proposed the Inclusive Wealth Index (IWI).

Name: Partha Dasgupta
Role: Directed the development of the Inclusive Wealth Index, integrating ecological and social capital into a single metric for national wellbeing.
Description: Economist who led the United Nations University effort on the Inclusive Wealth Index.
Supporting_Text: The United Nations University, under the leadership of Partha Dasgupta, proposed the Inclusive Wealth Index (IWI).

Name: Maryland
Role: Implemented GPI at the state level, providing a concrete example of replacing GDP with a welfare‑oriented metric that accounts for environmental and social factors.
Description: U.S. state government that has adopted an official Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) measure.
Supporting_Text: Two US states, Maryland and Vermont, have introduced official GPI measures

Name: Vermont
Role: Implemented GPI at the state level, providing a concrete example of replacing GDP with a welfare‑oriented metric that accounts for environmental and social factors.
Description: U.S. state government that has adopted an official Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) measure.
Supporting_Text: Two US states, Maryland and Vermont, have introduced official GPI measures

Name: UN representatives
Role: Convinced Amartya Sen to adopt a simplified version of his capability approach for the HDI, facilitating the creation of a widely used alternative to GDP.
Description: Officials and delegates of the United Nations who engage in policy formulation and advocacy.
Supporting_Text: Nevertheless, he was convinced by the UN representatives to go ahead with a highly simplified version of his theory.

Name: Amartya Sen
Role: Provided the theoretical foundation (capability approach) that informed the design of the Human Development Index, a key Beyond‑GDP metric that values human wellbeing beyond monetary output.
Description: Indian economist and philosopher, originator of the capability approach to welfare economics.
Supporting_Text: The capability approach is philosophically challenging and critiques welfare economics in particular. Sen was not in fact in favour of capturing the many dimensions of society in one index.

Name: World Economic Forum
Role: Produces composite indicators such as the Competitiveness Index, which, while not explicitly a Beyond‑GDP tool, exemplifies the broader use of multi‑dimensional metrics in economic discourse.
Description: Swiss‑based international organization that publishes global competitiveness and innovation rankings.
Supporting_Text: Examples include the Competitiveness Index published by the World Economic Forum and the Global Innovation Index.

Name: King of Bhutan
Role: Initiated one of the earliest and most cited Beyond‑GDP initiatives (Gross National Happiness) in the early 1970s, providing a concrete alternative to GDP‑based measurement.
Description: Monarch of Bhutan who launched the Gross National Happiness programme.
Supporting_Text: One of the earliest and most cited Beyond-GDP initiatives is the programme on Gross National Happiness which was initiated by the King of Bhutan in the early 1970s.

Name: Commission for Sustainable Development (CSD)
Role: Proposed a Type 3 indicator set in 1995 and facilitated stakeholder deliberations among UN member states, giving a major boost to the measurement of Beyond‑GDP metrics.
Description: A United Nations commission established to promote sustainable development indicators.
Supporting_Text: In 1995 the Commission for Sustainable Development (CSD) proposed such an indicator set. The CSD indicators were based on stakeholder deliberations between the various countries of the UN.

Name: EU28 countries
Role: Each created its own national indicator set, demonstrating both diffusion of Beyond‑GDP metrics and divergence from the CSD benchmark.
Description: The 28 member states of the European Union (as of the period discussed).
Supporting_Text: All EU28 countries created their own indicator set, and there was also a European SDI which was produced by Eurostat.

Name: Switzerland
Role: Early adopter of Type 4 (conceptual) sustainability indicator sets, contributing to the shift toward incorporating nature’s value in economic metrics.
Description: A European country that began creating indicator sets based on conceptual frameworks in the mid‑2000s.
Supporting_Text: in the mid-2000s a couple of countries started to create indicator sets based on conceptual frameworks: Switzerland, Norway and New Zealand

Name: New Zealand
Role: Early adopter of Type 4 (conceptual) sustainability indicator sets, influencing the integration of wellbeing‑based metrics beyond GDP.
Description: A Pacific nation that began creating indicator sets based on conceptual frameworks in the mid‑2000s.
Supporting_Text: in the mid-2000s a couple of countries started to create indicator sets based on conceptual frameworks: Switzerland, Norway and New Zealand

Name: Belgium
Role: Expanded the use of conceptual sustainability indicators, supporting the move toward metrics that value nature and wellbeing.
Description: A European country that later introduced Type 4 indicator sets.
Supporting_Text: Later the Netherlands and Belgium also introduced Type 4 indicator sets

Name: UNECE
Role: Co‑creator of the Working Group for Statistics on Sustainable Development (WGSSD) and later the Task Force on Measuring Sustainable Development (TFSD), driving the development of nature‑inclusive statistical frameworks.
Description: United Nations Economic Commission for Europe, an intergovernmental body.
Supporting_Text: In 2004, the UNECE, OECD and Eurostat (European Commission) created the Working Group for Statistics on Sustainable Development (WGSSD)

Name: Working Group for Statistics on Sustainable Development (WGSSD)
Role: Produced a 2009 report that influenced the Stiglitz Report and promoted both monetary and non‑monetary indicators for natural and other capital.
Description: A joint UNECE‑OECD‑Eurostat working group established in 2004 to develop sustainability statistics.
Supporting_Text: In 2004, the UNECE, OECD and Eurostat (European Commission) created the Working Group for Statistics on Sustainable Development (WGSSD).

Name: Joint UNECE/OECD/Eurostat Task Force on Measuring Sustainable Development (TFSD)
Role: Built on the Stiglitz Report’s conceptual framework and produced Type 4 indicator sets, further embedding nature’s value into statistical systems.
Description: Successor task force to the WGSSD, created in 2009 to advance measurement of sustainable development.
Supporting_Text: In 2009, just after the publication of the Stiglitz Report, the joint UNECE/OECD/Eurostat Task Force on Measuring Sustainable Development (TFSD) was created.

Name: Conference of European Statisticians
Role: Endorsed the TFSD report, facilitating adoption of sustainability indicators by European countries.
Description: A professional body that brings together national statistical institutes across Europe.
Supporting_Text: The report was endorsed by the Conference of European Statisticians and the CES Recommendations on Measuring Sustainable Development have been adopted by a couple of countries so far.

Name: Statistical Commission of the United Nations
Role: Adopted the SEEA 2012 Central Framework, thereby formalising the accounting system that can replace or complement GDP with environmental and natural‑capital metrics.
Description: The highest decision‑making body of the United Nations Statistical Commission, responsible for setting global statistical standards.
Supporting_Text: After a lengthy deliberation process the System of Environmental Economic Accounting 2012 - Central Framework was adopted by the Statistical Commission of the United Nations.

Name: UN Statistical Division
Role: Set an explicit target for a hundred countries to start producing SEEA accounts by 2020, driving the diffusion of nature‑centric metrics worldwide.
Description: A division of the United Nations that supports the development and implementation of global statistical standards and capacity‑building.
Supporting_Text: The UN Statistical Division has made it its explicit aim to have a hundred countries start producing SEEA account by 2020.

Name: Statistical offices of UN member states
Role: Agreed to adopt the SEEA handbook, enabling the production of environmental accounts that integrate nature’s value into national economic statistics.
Description: National statistical agencies of the United Nations' member countries responsible for collecting and reporting official statistics.
Supporting_Text: Getting this handbook agreed by six international institutes and all the statistical offices of the UN member states is a major achievement.

Name: US Congress
Role: Discontinued the United States' environmental accounts, illustrating vested institutional resistance to Beyond‑GDP initiatives.
Description: The legislative body of the United States that discontinued the environmental accounts in the 1990s.
Supporting_Text: The environmental accounts of the United States were discontinued in the 1990s by the US Congress.

Name: Bleys
Role: Provided a comprehensive assessment of requirements (timeliness, robustness, communication, standardised methodology) for successful Beyond‑GDP adoption.
Description: Co‑author of a 2015 assessment of Beyond‑GDP initiatives.
Supporting_Text: Bleys and Whitby (2015) probably provide the most comprehensive assessment in this direction.

Name: Whitby
Role: Co‑authored the comprehensive assessment of success criteria for Beyond‑GDP indicators.
Description: Co‑author of a 2015 assessment of Beyond‑GDP initiatives.
Supporting_Text: Bleys and Whitby (2015) probably provide the most comprehensive assessment in this direction.

Name: Hayden
Role: Investigated the disappointing uptake of Beyond‑GDP indicators, highlighting implementation challenges.
Description: Co‑author of a 2016 study on the uptake of Beyond‑GDP indicators in Canada.
Supporting_Text: Hayden and Wilson (2016) investigate the disappointing" uptake of Beyond‑GDP indicators in Canada."

Name: Wilson
Role: Co‑investigated the limited adoption of Beyond‑GDP metrics, contributing to the critique of current approaches.
Description: Co‑author of a 2016 study on the uptake of Beyond‑GDP indicators in Canada.
Supporting_Text: Hayden and Wilson (2016) investigate the disappointing" uptake of Beyond‑GDP indicators in Canada."

Name: Costanza et al.
Role: Proposed analogies between GDP addiction and substance addiction, suggesting motivational interviewing as a possible societal intervention.
Description: Research team led by Robert Costanza that authored a 2017 paper linking society’s GDP focus to addiction.
Supporting_Text: In a novel paper, Costanza et al. (2017) liken society's focus on economic growth to a real addiction.
